messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] problem met in vol1 example Leuk
parts:
> On Thu, Dec 8, 2011 at 12:53 PM, Jiqiang Guo<guo...@gmail.com> wrote:
>> Error message during running:
>>
>> Exception: Error in function stan::prob::normal_log<d>(d): Random
>> variate x is -nan, but must be finite!

This is exciting -- we're printing reasonable
messages for errors already.

Given that the only normal in the model is

beta ~ normal(0, 10);

and the beta isn't declared to be transformed, the beta
parameter had to come in as a NaN value. I don't see how
this could come about -- the only thing that happens to it
is adding momentum amounts and the gradient of normal_log(0,10)
shouldn't be too sharp.

Is it repeatable, Daniel? It always goes to NaN
in the second step?

One issue is whether we then want to just catch
these exceptions in the sampler loop, report
them, then try again (up to some limit so we
don't go into an infinite loop).

I'm not sure what JAGS does, but I've often seen
pages and pages of error messages about NaN values
found in evaluations (usually in gamma functions).

- Bob

messages.author: ab7b24da45678eac
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] problem met in vol1 example Leuk
parts:
In this example, some of the likelihood items would be from
0 ~ poisson(0) if Y[i, j] = 0, which should not be specified at all.  
How Bugs deals with it?  

So if I change the cpp code (for the time being) from 

lp__ += stan::prob::poisson_log(dN[i - 1][j - 1], ((Y[i - 1][j - 1] * exp((beta * Z[i - 1]))) * dL0[j - 1]));

to: 

 if (Y[i - 1][j - 1] > 0)
        lp__ += stan::prob::poisson_log(dN[i - 1][j - 1], ((Y[i - 1][j - 1] * exp((beta * Z[i - 1]))) * dL0[j - 1]));

I guess we would have the correct result (only checked one parameter).

That's easier to fix. In fact, we want to determine
all these boundary conditions that might pop up.

We can set

poisson_log(N,lambda)
= 0.0 if N = 0, lambda = 0.0
= error if N > 0, lambda = 0.0
= error if lambda < 0 or N < 0
= business as usual otherwise

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] problem met in vol1 example Leuk
parts:
Great.  I checked the PMF function of Poisson in R, which 
gives 

> dpois(1, lambda = 0)
[1] 0
> dpois(0, lambda = 0)
[1] 1
> dpois(2, lambda = 0)
[1] 0
> dpois(-2, lambda = 0)
[1] 0

So it might be better that when lambda=0, 
poisson_log(N, lambda) gives log(0) when N is not 0. 
I am not sure about this since even I am not sure about 
log(0) is legitimate. 


--
Jiqiang

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: bounds checking, part two
parts:
On 12/8/11 4:08 PM, Jiqiang Guo wrote:
> > dpois(1, lambda = 0)
> [1] 0
> > dpois(0, lambda = 0)
> [1] 1
> > dpois(2, lambda = 0)
> [1] 0
> > dpois(-2, lambda = 0)
> [1] 0

That makes sense mathematically if you
think of Poisson(N|lambda) being defined over
all integers for all N no matter what lambda is.
I think Boost has the same kind of behavior.

Also, we're following Mssrs. Gelman, Carlin, Stern,
and Rubin, the appendix of whose book states
that Poisson(N|lambda) is defined for lambda > 0 (strictly)
and N = 0, 1, 2, ...

The problem is that even if lambda is a parameter
which we bound > 0, we can get 0 due to underflow
when we do the exp(x) reverse transform for
x < -400 or so.

We also need gradients. The problem is
that poisson_log(N,lambda) doesn't have a gradient
if N is negative, or if lambda is not greater than
zero.

We also want to be more helpful in flagging client
errors. If they put in count data with negative
counts, we want to trap it as early as possible as
an error.

Another issue for us is that we want to be able
to

Like Boost, R handles the RHS differently.

> dpois(-2,-2)
[1] NaN
Warning message:
In dpois(x, lambda, log) : NaNs produced

Unlike Boost, R would make Matt happy, because it
treats the location and sampled value symmetrically.
Boost complains if you do y ~ norm(mu,sigma) with
anything but a finite mu, though it'll allow infinite y.
(That makes sense given their design because they
construct an object for norm(mu,sigma) and catch the
error at construction time if you've used illegal
parameters.)

> So it might be better that when lambda=0,
> poisson_log(N, lambda) gives log(0) when N is not 0.
> I am not sure about this since even I am not sure about
> log(0) is legitimate.

log(0) produces -infinity in IEEE arithmetic.
We'd like to make sure our distribution code handles
the infinities well, too. For instance, R also does
sensible things with all the infinity cases for the normal:

> dnorm(1/0,0,1)
[1] 0
>
> dnorm(1/0,0,1,log=T)
[1] -Inf
> dnorm(0,1/0,1)
[1] 0
> dnorm(0,1/0,1,log=T)
[1] -Inf
> dnorm(0,0,1/0)
[1] 0
> dnorm(0,0,0/1)
[1] Inf

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Poisson bounds checking
parts:
On 12/8/11 4:52 PM, Daniel Lee wrote:
> I think at the end of that, we've decided that:
> lambda == 0 (regardless of N) is a domain error?
> or is it
> lamdba == 0 when N> 0 is a domain error?

Here's my thinking:

log_poisson(n,lambda)

= log Poisson(n|lambda) if +infinity > lambda > 0 and n >= 0

= domain error if lambda < 0 or n < 0

= domain error if n is NaN or lambda is NaN

The NaN error and other errors may just lead to
NaN propagation with the right traits set.

That leaves a few boundary conditions undecided.

= domain error if lambda = +infinity

If it were zero, the partial derivative w.r.t. lambda is
-infinity, and when we do +infinity + -infinity, we'll
get a NaN. So I think it's safe to leave this
an error.

= 0 if n = 0, lambda = 0

Just branching and returning 0 makes the gradient 0,
too. It could also throw an error.

= domain error if n > 0, lambda = 0

This could return -infinity if the gradient
makes sense:

lim(L -> 0) d/d.lambda log Poisson(n|lambda)

I didn't work through whether this limit makes
sense or blows up. The gradient would probably
have to be plumbed in by hand.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Poisson bounds checking
parts:
The limit values that the Poisson log-pdf actually gives in those last
few scenarios are
lambda=0, n=0: logp=0, grad_lambda=–1 (because 0log0 is basically 0)
lambda=0, n>0: logp=-inf, grad_lambda=inf (for one thing, because
log(1-1)=-inf and log(1-1+epsilon)>-inf)
lambda=inf, n<inf: logp=-inf, grad_lambda=-inf (because
log(gamma(lambda)) grows much faster than n*log(lambda))
lambda=inf, n=inf: domain error

Matt

Thanks. We've got some limits to calc along with
a whole bunch of cdf gradients.

I didn't work through the actual limits before, but
my intuition was that poisson(n|lambda) would converge
to a delta function as n->0 and lambda->0.

0 log 0 is another case we might want to build
into our auto-diff. There's no way to get this
out of basic log evaluation, though, because log(0) is
negative infinity and you evaluate compositionally.

Now if we had expression templates we might be able
to make it fly, but even then, it's a semantic not
a syntactic calc for the value of x in log(x) unless
the x is a structural 0 in a model somewhere.

- Bob
